title: Nevada clears Tesla, Waymo, and Uber to run up to 8,000 robotaxis in Clark County
subtitle: The Nevada Transportation Authority granted three commercial permits — Tesla up to 5,000 vehicles, Waymo and Uber up to 1,000 each — making Las Vegas the largest paid driverless service area in the U.S.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Nevada Transportation Authority unanimously approved three commercial robotaxi permits on August 20, covering Tesla, Waymo, and Uber for operations across Clark County — home to Las Vegas. Tesla was cleared for up to 5,000 vehicles, Waymo for up to 1,000, and Uber for another 1,000 that it plans to run through its Motional and Zoox partners. The permits also allow expansion statewide if the operators notify the commission first, and access to Harry Reid International Airport pending a separate Clark County Aviation sign-off.

The single-jurisdiction cap now sits at roughly 8,000 driverless vehicles for paid service — a step-change from the pilot-scale permits U.S. cities have granted so far. Waymo has been running commercial service in Phoenix and parts of California for years, but usually with fleets numbered in the hundreds and route geofences drawn tight. Nevada's approval opens a metro to three operators at once, at a fleet size that starts to look like an actual replacement for a rideshare workforce rather than a demonstration.

This is the first American city where the question shifts from 'will regulators allow this' to 'will demand and reliability match the permitted capacity.' Tesla's approval is especially notable because its unsupervised Full Self-Driving stack has faced more skepticism from state regulators than Waymo's lidar-plus-camera approach; getting to 5,000 vehicles in Clark County will force a public data set on how each stack performs at scale, side by side, on the same streets.

For learners, watch the incident and disengagement statistics that will now be reported publicly under Nevada's permit conditions. Robotaxi debates for the last five years have mostly been theoretical — arguments about miles per intervention, extrapolated from small fleets. A metro with 8,000 vehicles from three operators generates enough real-world data to settle a lot of those arguments within a year, one way or the other.
